title: Daily Practice Problems (DPP) — JEE Main & Advanced Maths: Trigonometry & Its Applications
meta_title: JEE Trigonometry DPP: Daily Practice Problems + Quiz
meta_desc: JEE trigonometry daily practice: ratios, identities, equations, inverse trig and heights and distances, plus a free 8-question JEE-level quiz.
excerpt: Trigonometry is where a lot of JEE aspirants quietly leak marks — not because it is hard, but because they never drill it daily. Here is how a trig DPP routine actually works, the sub-topics that get tested, and an 8-question quiz to check where you stand.
author: Sachin Sharma
content:
Give a JEE aspirant the equation 2sin²θ − 3sinθ + 1 = 0 and most will solve the quadratic correctly, find sinθ = 1 or ½, and then write down two answers instead of the full general solution. That single slip — forgetting that trigonometric equations have infinitely many roots — costs marks in nearly every JEE paper. Trigonometry is rarely the toughest topic on the syllabus, yet it quietly leaks more marks than calculus, and the reason is almost always the same: aspirants read the theory once and never drill it. That is exactly the gap a good set of Daily Practice Problems (DPP) closes.

I have watched students go from dreading the trig section to finishing it in under twenty minutes, and the change was never a new shortcut. It was ten problems a day, every day, for a few weeks. Below is why that works, the sub-topics JEE actually tests, a routine you can start tonight, and the traps that catch even strong students.

Why daily practice problems beat marathon sessions

Trigonometry is a memory-plus-reflex subject. You need the identities in long-term memory, but you also need the reflex to recognise which identity a problem is begging for. Reflexes are built by spacing, not cramming. A three-hour Sunday session gives you volume; ten problems every day gives you retrieval — and retrieval is what the brain rewards with retention.

The other quiet advantage of a DPP is mixing. A well-built daily set does not hand you eight identity questions in a row; it gives you one identity, one equation, one inverse-trig, one heights-and-distances. That forces you to first decide what kind of problem this is before you solve it — which is precisely the decision you must make in the real exam, where questions arrive unlabelled.

The trigonometry sub-topics JEE tests

JEE Main and Advanced draw trigonometry from five clearly separable buckets. Knowing which bucket a question sits in is half the battle.

  • Trigonometric ratios & identities — the foundation: values on the unit circle, compound-angle and multiple-angle formulae, and conditional identities where A + B + C = π.
  • Trigonometric equations — finding the general solution, not just the principal value; this is the single most tested sub-topic and the one most often botched.
  • Inverse trigonometric functions — domains, ranges (this is where sign errors live), and the addition formulae for tan⁻¹ that must be adjusted outside the standard range.
  • Heights and distances — the applications: angles of elevation and depression, usually solved with a clean sine or tangent ratio and a careful diagram.
  • Properties of triangles — the sine and cosine rules, area formulae, the in-radius r and circum-radius R, and projection formulae; a favourite of JEE Advanced.

A trig DPP routine that actually sticks

Ten to twelve problems a day is the sweet spot — enough to build reflex, short enough that you never skip it. Rotate the emphasis across the week so no bucket goes cold.

DayFocusSample problem type
MonRatios & identitiesProve or simplify a compound-angle expression
TueTrigonometric equationsGeneral solution of a quadratic-in-sinθ
WedInverse trigEvaluate tan⁻¹x + tan⁻¹y with a range check
ThuHeights & distancesTwo-angle observation of a tower
FriProperties of trianglesSine rule / cosine rule application
SatMixed set (timed)All five buckets, 25 minutes
SunError log reviewRedo only the ones you got wrong

The Sunday step is the one people skip, and it is the most valuable. Keep an error log — a plain notebook page where every wrong answer gets one line: the problem type and why you missed it. After three weeks you will notice your mistakes cluster into two or three patterns, and fixing a pattern fixes dozens of future problems at once.

Common traps that cost JEE marks

Writing principal values instead of general solutions

If a question asks to solve sinθ = ½, the answer is θ = nπ + (−1)ⁿ(π/6), not merely π/6. Losing the general form is the number-one trig error in JEE Main.

Ignoring the range of inverse functions

tan⁻¹x + tan⁻¹y = tan⁻¹((x+y)/(1−xy)) only holds when xy < 1. Outside that, you add or subtract π. Advanced loves this exact trap.

Squaring an equation and importing extra roots

Squaring to clear a square root or combine terms can introduce solutions that do not satisfy the original equation. Always substitute your answers back before you commit.

Domain restrictions on identities

An identity you divided by cosθ is invalid wherever cosθ = 0. Check the boundary angles; JEE Advanced plants questions precisely at those excluded points.

How to use a ready-made DPP set

Building your own daily sets is possible but slow, and you will unconsciously avoid the problem types you dislike — which are exactly the ones you need. A curated DPP book solves that: it sequences the difficulty, mixes the buckets for you, and gives worked solutions so your error log stays honest. Treat the solutions as a last resort, not a first read; attempt every problem cold, mark the ones that beat you, and revisit them on Sunday.

Test where your trigonometry stands

Before you commit to a daily plan, find out which of the five buckets is your weakest. The free eight-question quiz below is pitched at JEE Main level and spans ratios, identities, equations, inverse trig, and heights and distances. Attempt each one honestly, then read the explanations for anything you miss. When you are ready for full daily sets with worked solutions, the trigonometry DPP e-book linked at the end takes it from there.

quiz.title: JEE Trigonometry DPP Quiz
quiz.intro: Eight JEE Main-level questions across ratios, identities, equations, inverse trig and heights and distances. Choose an answer for each, then press Check my score.

questions.q: The general solution of sinθ = ½ is:
questions.explanation: For sinθ = sinα, the general solution is θ = nπ + (−1)ⁿα. With α = π/6 this gives option (a). The 2nπ ± form is for cosine.

questions.q: If A + B + C = π, then tanA + tanB + tanC equals:
questions.explanation: When A + B + C = π, the identity tanA + tanB + tanC = tanA tanB tanC holds. It comes from tan(A+B) = tan(π − C).
sin75° = sin(45° + 30°) = sin45cos30 + cos45sin30 = (√6 + √2)/4. Note (a) is the value of sin15°.

questions.q: The number of solutions of 2sin²θ − 3sinθ + 1 = 0 in [0, 2π) is:
questions.explanation: Factor to (2sinθ − 1)(sinθ − 1) = 0, so sinθ = ½ (giving π/6 and 5π/6) or sinθ = 1 (giving π/2). That is three solutions.
This classic identity equals π. Note that tan⁻¹2 + tan⁻¹3 = π − π/4 because the product 2×3 > 1 forces a +π adjustment; adding tan⁻¹1 = π/4 gives π.

questions.q: The angle of elevation of the top of a tower from a point is 30°. Moving 40 m closer, it becomes 60°. The height of the tower is:
questions.explanation: With h = x tan60 and h = (x + 40) tan30, solving gives x = 20 and h = 20√3 m ≈ 34.6 m.

questions.q: In a triangle, a = 7, b = 8, c = 9. By the cosine rule, cosA equals:

questions.explanation: For a sinθ + b cosθ, the maximum is √(a² + b²) = √(9 + 16) = √25 = 5.

faq.q: How many trigonometry problems should I solve daily for JEE?
faq.a: Ten to twelve mixed problems a day is the sweet spot — enough to build recognition reflex without becoming a chore you skip. Consistency over several weeks matters far more than the occasional long session.

faq.q: Which trigonometry sub-topic is most important for JEE Main?
faq.a: Trigonometric equations, specifically the general solution. It appears in almost every paper and is the most commonly botched because students stop at the principal value. Master the nπ and 2nπ forms early.

faq.q: Is trigonometry weightage higher in JEE Main or Advanced?
faq.a: JEE Main tends to ask two to three direct trigonometry questions, often on equations and identities. Advanced asks fewer standalone questions but weaves properties of triangles and inverse trig into multi-concept problems, so the depth required is greater.

faq.q: How do I stop making sign errors in inverse trigonometry?
faq.a: Always write down the range of each inverse function before you apply an addition formula. The tan⁻¹ addition rule needs a ±π correction when the product of the arguments exceeds 1 — check that condition every single time.
